item.title: A Nagoya Meshi Food Tour: Eating Through Japan's Boldest Food City — Guide
item.description: No Japanese city guards a food identity as fiercely as Nagoya, whose ‘Nagoya meshi’ canon — eel hitsumabushi, miso-sauced katsu, peppery tebasaki wings, clay-pot miso nikomi udon, morning ogura toast and more — grew from the region’s dark hatcho miso and tamari brewing traditions into a cuisine found nowhere else. Eating through it is the city’s best itinerary: a self-guided day can run from kissaten breakfast through a noodle lunch to an izakaya wing crawl, while guided evening food tours thread the lantern-lit alleys and counter bars with a local who knows which queue is worth it.

item.title: Hitsumabushi: Nagoya's Three-Way Eel Feast — Guide
item.description: Hitsumabushi is the flagship of ‘Nagoya meshi’, the city’s proudly idiosyncratic food culture, and it turns grilled eel into a ritual of three acts: finely sliced, crisp-grilled unagi arrives on rice in a lacquered wooden tub, and you eat the first quarter plain, the second with wasabi, spring onion and shredded nori, and the third drowned in hot dashi as a fragrant ochazuke — before finishing with a fourth portion in whichever style won.

item.title: Miso Katsu: Nagoya's Dark-Sauced Tonkatsu — Guide
item.description: Miso katsu is Nagoya’s answer to tonkatsu: a crisp, golden pork cutlet draped in a glossy deep-brown sauce built on hatcho miso, the intensely savoury soybean miso that has been aged for years in giant cedar barrels near Okazaki since the age of the shoguns. The sauce — sweet, earthy and almost chocolatey in its depth — soaks gently into the panko crust and transforms the dish into the region’s definitive comfort food, served everywhere from the famous Yabaton chain with its pig mascot to old kissaten and department-store restaurants.

item.title: Tebasaki: Nagoya's Peppery Glazed Chicken Wings — Guide
item.description: Tebasaki are Nagoya’s iconic chicken wings: fried crisp without batter, brushed while hot with a sweet-savoury tare glaze, then hit hard with white pepper, salt and sesame, producing a lacquered, peppery crunch that has made them the city’s definitive beer food. The style was born at the restaurant Furaibo in the 1960s, and its friendly rivalry with the cheekier chain Yamachan — whose wings bite back with even more pepper — divides the city into loyal camps that visitors are honour-bound to adjudicate over a cold beer.
